newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish, Ukrainian leaders plan closer links.
newsitem.headline: Polish, Ukrainian leaders plan closer links.

text.p: Presidents Leonid Kuchma of Ukraine and Aleksander Kwasniewski of Poland outlined plans on Thursday to step up political and economic exchanges this year to cement warm ties both see as crucial to their region.
They oversaw the signing of a memorandum, like one Poland clinched with Russia last year, on their desire to liberalise trade and create a mutual free trade zone in the future.

Kuchma was invited to Warsaw by the Polish Business Club employers group to receive a man of the year award for market reforms that have boosted bilateral trade and he took the chance for talks with Kwasniewski, alone and then with advisers.

Poland, on course for its top goals of joining the European Union and NATO, restated it would be a tireless advocate for its larger ex-Soviet neighbour's efforts to bind itself to Central and Western European groupings.

Kwasniewski promised to back Ukraine's aim of reaching an association agreement with the EU and joining the Central European Free Trade Agreement (CEFTA) and he offered Polish experts' advice for Ukraine's economic reforms.

He said the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation should reach a special charter with Ukraine, like that which it is discussing with Russia -- a country that, unlike Ukraine, opposes NATO's expansion to embrace Poland.

"I think an enlarged NATO should have an appropriate, separate treaty with Ukraine, because without Ukraine it is hard to imagine a system of common European security," Kwasniewski told a news conference after the talks.
"I thank you very much for your understanding and support," said Kuchma.

The presidents set out proposals to increase growing economic ties, which Kuchma said would be carried further by Polish business representatives in Kiev this month and a March visit to Warsaw by Ukraine's Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko.

Poland's trade with Ukraine exceeded $1 billion for the first time in 1995 and totalled $1.4 billion from January to September last year, a rise of 39 percent over the same period of 1995, according to Polish Economy Ministry figures.

The data, quoted by PAP news agency, showed the balance of trade firmly in Poland's favour, with exports totalling $1 billion in the first nine months of 1996 and consisting mainly of chemicals, coal, food products and electronics.

Poland, which imports mainly iron ore, chemicals and grain from Ukraine, also has investments in some 400 firms there and Kuchma said a planned tax reform would encourage further investment by Poland's fast-growing economy.

Polish-Ukrainian relations have historically been troubled and both countries are drafting a declaration of reconciliation on painful issues, including a grim revolt by Ukrainians in east Poland after World War Two which Warsaw's then-communist authorities ended by a harsh mass deportation.
Kwasniewski said he was sure the document, settling the past to prepare for a positive future, would be ready for adoption when he visited Kiev officially in May.

Both presidents, who with Lithuania's Algirdas Brazauskas voiced concern for democracy in Belarus when President Alexander Lukashenko clashed with parliament last year, said it was important not to isolate it the country.
"If Poland and Ukraine turn their backs on Belarus, Belarus will have a road open only to Moscow," Kwasniewski said.
Both said they did not oppose closer Belarussian economic and political integration with Russia but backed the existence of a sovereign Belarus.
